subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PRICE FOR 1948-49 CROP TEAR

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PRICE FOR 1948-49 CROP TEAR
speechtext: I wish to make an announcement concerning the 1948 crop of flaxseed. The government has been advised that to meet our domestic requirements we can do with a somewhat smaller acreage of flaxseed than was sown last year. There are some definite signs of easing in the world situation on oil bearing seeds and distinct possibilities that we will no longer have the serious shortage that we have been facing for the past several years. With this changing situation in mind, it has been decided that the Canadian wheat board will be instructed to support prices of $4 per bushel for the top grades of flaxseed, basis delivered at Montreal or basis in store at Fort William/Port Arthur for the 1948-49 crop year commencing next August 1, should the market drop to that level. On the same date, the wartime prices and trade board ceiling of $5 per bushel will be removed, thus permitting buyer and seller to trade freely at prices above the support levels. In any event, the producers sowing flaxseed this year will be sure of a price not less than $4 per bushel for top grades.

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Mr. HOWARD C. GREEN (Vancouver South): I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. Press dispatches of the last day or two indicate that militia ranger units are to be established in northern Canada. Will the minister make a statement with regard to this proposal and indicate whether or not that will include northern British Columbia?

speakeroldname: Hon. BROOKE CLAXTON (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF CANADIAN RANGERS AS CORPS OF CANADIAN ARMY
speechtext: I should like to have had time to get full information for the hon. member. Speaking from memory I can say that last April when I was in Vancouver I announced the formation of the Canadian rangers as a corps of the Canadian army, to be organized on the general pattern of the Pacific coast rangers during the second world war. The intention is that this corps shall be organized in companies in areas where there are no reserve army units, particularly in the north and along the coasts of Canada. The purpose will be to act as guides, to make available local knowledge, to assist in search and rescue work, and to report any activities that should not be going on in consequence of action by an enemy, or the like. These men in the Canadian rangers will be issued a rifle, bayonet, belt, and some ammunition, and they will have training in their companies in line with the kind of work they are intended to do. In this way it is hoped to supplement the work which the reserve army units do in the more organized centres of population.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO PROSECUTION OF DENTAL FIRMS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO PROSECUTION OF DENTAL FIRMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker I undertook yesterday, in response to a question by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), to give the house a statement today respecting the circumstances surrounding the recent dismissal by a Toronto court of the crown's case against members of an alleged combine in the dental supplies trade. Since the matter is

still open to appeal and thus is or shortly may be sub judice, hon. members will not expect me to make any extended comment on the case at this time.
Following a report by the commissioner of the Combines Investigation Act, I referred the matter for prosecution to Mr. D. L. McCarthy, K.C., of Toronto, whom all members will recognize as, one of the outstanding barristers of the dominion. He was ably assisted by two experienced Toronto counsel, Messrs. Peter Wright and D. A. Keith.
A charge was laid at Toronto against eighteen dental supply companies for conspiracy in undue restraint of trade. The trial began on February 23 and ended on March 18. The crown's case was based on more than five hundred documents seized under search warrant from the possession of the accused companies. No evidence was submitted by the defence, and after argument lasting almost three days the learned trial judge, the Honourable Mr. Justice Barlow, upheld the defence motion for a directed verdict and directed the jury to enter a verdict of not guilty.
Acquittal was not based on the information contained in the documents found in the possession of the accused companies, but followed the judge's ruling that the documents had not been sufficiently authenticated by the fact of possession, as claimed by the crown. According to the ruling, the crown should have proved specifically that the companies actually existed during the period of the charge, that the persons purportedly acting on behalf of them actually had authority to act, and that signatures of persons signing letters should have been proved by other evidence.
The eminent counsel acting for the crown proceeded with full confidence in the merits of the case disclosed by the documents and in the manner in which they were proved. Withdrawal of the case from the jury resulted not from inadvertence or unintentional omission on the part of crown counsel, but from a basic difference of opinion as to the rules of evidence to be applied.
In view of the importance of the matter and its possible implications affecting future cases under the Combines Investigation Act, I have asked Mr. McCarthy for a special report. Until I have received and considered it, I shall not be in a position to indicate what may be done by way of appeal or otherwise.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO PROSECUTION OF DENTAL FIRMS
speechtext:
May I ask this supplementary question: After the crown's case had been concluded, is it not a fact that counsel asked to have the case reopened, as is

Inquiries oj the Ministry

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO PROSECUTION OF DENTAL FIRMS

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO PROSECUTION OF DENTAL FIRMS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 1949
speechtext:
This amendment to the Agricultural Products Act is to extend the bill for one year. I want to take this opportunity of voicing my disapproval once more of the principle of the bill. Our position has been stated clearly on previous occasions by my leader and also by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton). My exception to the principle of this bill is based on the fact that it is a price control measure, purely under government control and that it is not what it is supposed to be, namely a marketing bill. I say that because of the minister's own statement. He has admitted that to this house, and also on various occasions when speaking outside of the house. I would even go so far as to say that this bill could be used for political purposes to the disadvantage of many farmers across the country.
I want to say a word about the effect on farmers of this type of government control. I want to make it quite clear that the farmers of this country have never asked for all the traffic would bear for their produce, and that they are satisfied to support a measure of stability for the benefit of both producer and consumer. As a result of this bill, the farmers of Canada have been subsidizing not only the consumers of Canada but the consumers of the United Kingdom. They are not satisfied with the present one-way street method or this lopsided method which the government has taken unto itself. To prove that statement I just want to quote a couple of paragraphs from the resolutions passed by the Canadian federation of agriculture at Brock-ville. The first, which deals with ceiling prices, is as follows:
Protesting emphatically against the manifest injustice of the recently announced policy of 5849-160i
the federal government in singling out major agricultural products for the reimposition of ceiling prices without the reintroduction of a general policy of price control.
The next one is from the statement of the dairy farmers of Canada and is as follows:
If price controls are to be imposed on food products of which they are the primary producers, dairy farmers insist that controls be placed on all factors entering into their costs.
I say that the government has maintained on various occasions that the Agricultural Prices Support Act of 1944 was meant for this purpose, but it is not permanent legislation. The past experience of the potato growers, particularly in the eastern provinces of the dominion, has not made for good feeling on' the part of these growers through the operation and administration of this act. In the first place the act was not put into effect until practically the end of the potato marketing season. By that time the potatoes had shrunk to quite a large extent, they had sprouted and needed a good deal of sorting before they were made available to this board that was buying them. The farmers felt that the price was not sufficient to take care of all the work they were forced to do in order to market them. I maintain that it is the uncertainty in the minds of the farmers across the dominion that' is causing considerably lowered production, along with the effect of the income tax. After the farmers during all the war years had made an all-out effort to produce large quantities of food, and were successful in their objective, subsidizing the consumers of this country and of Great Britain, the government now comes along and says, "We are going to extract from you in income tax every nickel that we can." That greater production was largely brought about by overtime work. The farmer could not hope to produce the large quantities which were produced during the war in an eight-hour day and a five-day week. Is he going to continue to work that overtime in order to produce, with his markets as uncertain as they are today? I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that he is not; and production figures have shown definitely that he will not do so. [DOT]
I wish to put on Hansard certain figures from sessional paper 164A, dated March 8, but before doing so I would be glad to give the minister an opportunity to answer the question I asked on Friday night, because I think it would be only fair to do this.

That only bears out what I said regarding the lowering of production of three out of four of the agreements we have to supply Great Britain. Now what is the future of the hog producers of Canada? The only stipulation is that the price of 1949 shall not go below the 1946 figure. What is the 1946 figure? What was the price in 1946? It was $22.75 up until April 1 and it was raised to $25 on that day. Which of these two figures will be the 1946 minimum which is expected to be the contract price for 1949? That is the thing the farmers are asking today, and that is the thing that is keeping them from increasing the production of hogs. There is an uncertainty as regards the price, and uncertainty as regards the policy of this government. The lowering of production of all these products across Canada will mean that ultimately the consumer will have to pay higher prices for the food he buys. That will be the result indirectly, because when you lower production you will undoubtedly increase the cost to the consumer. So that by their policies

Agricultural Products Act
this government has greatly decreased production, which will mean ultimately that the consumer will pay more.
Another thing to which I would refer is this. Why are these contracts not available to the public? The minister said the other day it was because the contracts were not signed. After three months these contracts are still not signed by the contracting parties, and yet Mr. Taggart at a meeting of the Ontario hog producers in Toronto stated "firm as to quantity" when he was asked a question about bacon contracts. From that statement that the contract was firm as to quantity, I can only deduce he implies that the contract was not firm as to price. Under ordinary circumstances a businessman would not think that a contract which was not signed by both contracting parties was worth very much.
I hold in my hand a Canadian Press release reporting a statement by Mr. Strachey in England about these contracts. After seeing this statement I question just how much can be taken from the statement made in Toronto.
I will quote from this press clipping taken from the Globe and Mail of March 18, 1948. It is headed "Asks slash in U.K. buying from Canada." The text, dated at London, March 17. is as follows:
Britain's purchases from non-dollar countries must be increased and her present rate of spending on Canadian food cannot be continued, Food Minister John Strachey said today.
No complete cut-off in Canadian purchases was proposed as this would mean "disaster" to both countries, he said at a press conference.

Harold Wilson, president of the board of trade, told the Overseas Empire Correspondents' Association that even with the increased exports being directed to Canada, Britain would not be able to pay for all her minimum needs of Canadian goods. In Europe, Strachey said, "A whole series of negotiations for food have been undertaken in the past nine months and treaties under which we shall buy slowly but steadily increasing quantities of food have been concluded with Denmark, Poland, Holland, Italy, Hungary, Portugal, France, Spain, Iceland and Eire."

The minister may read that when he makes his reply. I want to go back to January 1947. The minister has made statements in the house, perhaps somewhat boastfully, that the marketing of hogs has improved considerably in the first two months of 1948. Let me say to him there is a reason for that. In January 1947, an artificially high price was paid by the packers for hogs in Canada which, rightly or wrongly, gave many farmers the impression that hog prices were going to stay at that abnormally high figure. Many of them did go into hogs at that time, and kept their sows instead of marketing them. They bred those sows, and of course last fall, when price controls went off feeds, many of the sows went back on the market. However there were others of them which did farrow, and the pigs which were farrowed are now coming on the market. I believe that is the reason for the great increase in hog marketings at the present time.
I have here statistics from the livestock survey of December 1, 1947. They show that the fall1 pig crop of 1947 was nine per cent less than that of 1946. The number of sows bred to farrow from December 1 to the month of May, 1948, was 67 per cent of those in the same periodl in the previous year. So that indications are that that increase in marketings at this stage of the year would not hold for more than probably a month at the outside.
Last year the minister said that the decrease was due to the scarcity of grain. Let me at this time quote from the quarterly review on Canadian coarse grains, the issue for February, 1948. I wonder what the minister will use as an excuse this year. This is what I find in this publication:
Visible supplies of both oats and' barley at February 19 are both in excess of the commercial supply position on the same date a year ago. Oats supplies at 30-2 million bushels exceed last year's figure by nearly a million bushels while barley stocks at 32-1 million are more than 11 million bushels greater than last year . . . Stocks of oats and barley located at eastern lake ports were reported on February 19 this year at 7'8 and 5-3 million bushels respectively. Last year only 3-4 million bushels of oats and IT million bushels of barley were at eastern lake ports. Lakehead stocks of barley at 11-5' million
Agricultural Products Act

bushels are also up 6 million bushels while lake-head oats stocks at 9-5 million bushels are nearly a million bushels greater than a year ago.
May I point out further that the hog-barley ratio as shown in this same review is placed at' 17*1, the same as it was in January 1946. However this is many points below the high of 21-4 of February 1947. So that the hog-barley ratio does not show there would) be a considerable increase in the production of . pork. '
Where do we go from here? It is my view, which can be verified, that the farmers of this country want enabling federal legislation so that producer boards operating in the provinces can have control of their own handling and marketing of produce. They would require legislation similar to that passed in 1934 by the Bennett government, legislation which was then known as the Natural Products Marketing Act. May I quote the following resolution on this point from the Canadian federation of agriculture:
Dominion marketing legislation:
Whereas the organized farmers of Canada, through the provincial and Canadian federations of agriculture, have on many occasions since the court decision that the 1934 marketing act was ultra vires, requested the dominion government to enact comprehensive marketing legislation that would enable farmers to market their products in an orderly manner;
And whereas the government nas not seen fit to pass such legislation and has not as yet given any logical reason why this request of the farmers should not be granted,
And whereas eight of the nine provinces of Canada have shown by their actions in passing provincial marketing legislation that, in their opinion, such legislation is necessary and in the public interest;
Therefore be it resolved:
1.	That the Canadian Federation of Agriculture again puts on record its belief that dominion marketing legislation, to supplement the provincial acts, is urgently necessary if the farmers of Canada are to be placed in a position equal to that of other elements in the com-jnunity.
2.	That, once more, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture requests the dominion government to introduce at the next session of parliament comprehensive marketing legislation that will make it possible for groups of farmers to control the marketing of their own products rather than be at the mercy of speculative interests.
3.	That failing assurances that such legislation will be introduced, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture demands to know the reasons why the government of Canada, by its lack of action in this important matter, is apparently of the opinion that the farmers of Canada should be kept permanently in an inferior position as compared with other elements of society, and that such reasons be published for the information of all Canadian farmers.

I think that is sufficient proof that the Canadian farmers do want that type of legislation.
I just want to say a word about the C.C.F. stand on this measure. They have given much lip service to that particular type of legislation, but on the other hand they seem to be satisfied with the legislation that is being passed today. In lieu of the marketing legislation which the farmers of this country do want I suggest that instead of having the price of hogs for the 1949 contract not set until probably the end of December 1948, a minimum and maximum price should be set two years in advance and reviewed each year. The farmers would then know one year in advance what their prices would be. There would be a minimum and maximum price, not just a question mark. No continuity of supply can be expected either by this government or by Great Britain if the farmers of this country do not know more about what their price is going to be in the future than they do today.

The statement which was put out at the time the contracts were entered into was to the effect that the financial arrangements were finally concluded, not only with regard to food products but with regard to other products, some of which have been named in this article in the press. The financial arrangements were completed down to the end of March. It was felt that by the end of March in all probability the Marshall plan would be operating. However, the British food contracts were not subject to that condition at all. The food contracts are hard and fast contracts for so much money at so much per unit. As I said the other day, the problem of arranging the means by which they are to make payment was a matter for parties other than the Minister of Agriculture to worry about.
The situation is that there is no question whatsoever that the British have enough dollars that they themselves could pay many times over the amounts required for the food they are getting from Canada and still have a considerable carryover of United States dollar? at the end of the year. That carryover may not be as great as they would desire to have, but there has never been any question about their having enough dollars to pay for food. From time to time they do discuss with us the extent to which we would agree to assist them in meeting their obligations and the extent to which they would agree to assisting us in meeting ours.
For example, we delivered far more bacon and far more beef under the contract in January and February than the contract called for, but the British took that beef and bacon. There had to be negotiations with them as to how the financing was to be handled within the terms of the contract, but they handled it. When they run into difficulties they come back to us and discuss the question. What I want to impress upon the house and particularly upon the farmers is that that contract is an absolutely closed contract, both with regard to price and with regard to quantities.

speechtext:
I had not intended to say anything at all on this measure other than to ask a question or two, because I have made my position clear in past sessions. But hon. members to my left seemed to be eager to take a long time in recording this this vote today. Therefore I intend to make a few observations with regard to this measure. First of all, I should like to remind the committee that in any democratic country which has turned to socialism the standard of living of the people has always been decreased. When we were discussing this measure a year ago we tried to move a number of amendments. After the principle of the Natural Products Marketing Act was passed, the government refused to accept any of those amendments. The two speakers from this party who today so well set out our position have pretty well proven the fact that this measure has not been, and is not working satisfactorily for the producers of this country. I have before me the Economic Annalist, a publication put out by the statistical bureau of the Department of Agriculture. It says that there has been a general decline in total meat production from the record level of 1944. and that the quantity of pork products available for export is

expected to decline throughout 1948. Then the Weekly Live Stock Market Review of March 12, 1948, states that exports of dairy cattle to the United States from January 1 to date-slightly over two months-has been 10,411 as compared with 5,433 in the corresponding period of last year. That is still going on to a greater degree than ever. It has been well said that we have today a far greater quantity of oats and barley in store in Canada than we had one year ago. We have a surplus of feed today; yet meat production is going down steadily, according to government records themselves. In the same issue of the Economic Annalist to which I referred a moment ago, at page 9, there is set out the situation at the present time with respect to the prairie farmers, as follows:
Although the prairie farmer is financially better off now than he was in 194.1, there is still room for improvement. Only 52 per cent of all farms reported owning one or more tractors; only 20 per cent reported having one or more trucks; and about 14 per cent reported possessing grain combines. The small proportion of farmers-four per cent-reporting ownership or possession of electric motors pointedly emphasizes the lack of such equipment.
Farmers have said that they want more machinery. Their farm buildings need to be repaired, repainted or rebuilt. Farm homes lack the many facilities essential to the wellbeing of the modern farm family. The exigencies of hazardous weather and crop failures have not been solved. Soil conservation is still a big problem. The prairie economy is still subject to the vagaries of the international market. The prosperity of the farmer on the prairies is still dependent upon a high and stable level of employment and income in Canada.
It goes on to say that at the present time there is a great deal of room for improvement. As regards the other side of the picture, I have here a letter I have received from a man who attended a large meeting, some 1,200 farmers, at Bismarck, North Dakota, and I should like to quote the following from it:
One glance at that audience of 1.200 farmers showed, without any further evidence, the difference in the prosperity between those farmers in North Dakota and our own farmers on these prairies. Our farmers are getting by without any question, that is, they are not going into debt but the prices they have received in the last four or five years have not permitted them to equip their farms with modern labour-saving machinery as they should have done, and have not enabled them to pay off fully their indebtedness and mortgages, and to put something by to tide them over for hard times. Over and over again farmers in North Dakota told me that a man seemed to feel and think quite differently if his debts were paid and he had a few dollars in the bank, compared to his state of mind when he was still in debt and had no reserves.

Agricultural Products Act
I know from my own practical experience that this is so, because I have taken occasion many times to visit North Dakota; and I can say that throughout the war years, and at the present time as well, our neighbours across the line in that state, compared with us in Manitoba, have had far better returns. They have had from two or three times more than we have. I have argued on many occasions that the general standard of living is higher across the line than it is in Canada and that the authorities in this country should endeavour to raise the living standards of the Canadian people.
I wish to say something on a matter that I have dealt with at every session since I have been here, following the year 1942, and that is the cattle embargo. I do not know how long we shall have to wait until that is lifted, but I know that the situation as pointed out in the Farm Ranch Review is far from satisfactory. I should like to quote the following from this publication. They are seriously asking for the exemption of pure breds from the live stock embargo. They say:
During the last two years an average of $8,090.0{!i0 worth of dairy stock have been exported annually to the United States. We are not arguing against this. [DOT]
It goes on:
Why not, then, encourage western farmers to devote their attention to purebred beef production by opening the American market to them? Why not make the same concession to the best beef raisers that is made to the best dairy stock raisers? They have rightly been given a chance to develop an American market. But the same opportunity being denied purebred beef producers.
The argument that this would denude the Canadian table of meat cannot be made to this suggestion. It would result, on the basis of the DBS. figures, to a resolution of 14 per cent in the Canadian meat supply.
How about it, Mr. Gardiner?
I emphasize the seriousness of this matter to the minister and to the government, and I would urge that the embargo be lifted as soon as possible in the interests of the producers of this country. As was ably pointed out by the hon. member for Brant, there has never been a time in the history of the country when our farm producers were so full of fear for the future as they are today. I cannot say whether there is a sound basis for that fear, but certainly the farmers and farm organizations have never been so fearful of their economic future as they are at the present time, and that statement is applicable throughout the country. They are certainly disappointed that they have not had greater access to the markets of the world. All this tends to make a peasantry of 5849-161-1
the future agricultural population of Canada as compared with the democracies throughout the world.
I could have taken up a good deal more time discussing this subject because there are some questions that I should like to have answered. I know, however, that the minister is eager to get the measure through this afternoon, and knowing the reasons behind that desire I will not take any more time just now. I simply wish to make our position and my own position as well quite clear to the committee, but I may have one or two other questions to ask before six o'clock.

speechtext:
The question with regard to cheese was how the floor price was determined. The floor price is set by the price at which we are prepared to buy cheese to send to Great Britain. That is, the dairy board purchases cheese at twenty-five cents under the old contract and at thirty cents under the new contract, basis Montreal and basis the plant. The cheese is purchased at that price and we undertake to buy all cheese that is delivered. So far as cheese is concerned, there is no great difficulty in determining what the floor should be. The cheese is purchased at the price set in the contract and sent to Britain.
With the ceiling off cheese, it can be sold on the Canadian market at a higher price. With regard to what was said a few moments ago, I should like to say that it was not the intention of the government at this time last year to requisition cheese. However we began to requisition cheese around July 1. I am not in position to state at the moment that there will be no requisitioning of cheese this year. We would rather not have to requisition cheese, but last year, when a quantity of cheese had been purchased by dealers sufficient to supply the Canadian market, we requisitioned what was left. Obviously the difference between beef and cheese is that cheese is a cured product which continues to get better for two or three years after it is made, while beef is an entirely different kind

Agricultural Products Act
of product. If we permitted anyone to buy all the cheese off the market this year he could store it and perhaps get a better price for it next year or the year after. He might lose on his speculation, but last year, when all the cheese was being bought and there was very little being turned in for export, after enough had been taken to supply this market we felt that the remainder ought to be taken at the guaranteed price and sent overseas.
We have no grading system in connection with beef cattle under which the beef is as carefully graded as cheese. Then, again, it is not the same kind of product. The floor price is set by the price in the British contract for beef. Taking into consideration the experiences over a long period of time, we can judge fairly closely as to what price cattle ought to be on the different markets across Canada; that is, what best steers ought to be and what lower grades of steers ought to be. The markets are checked daily in order to make certain that the price is at least as high as the floor price. We are not concerned with how much higher than the floor it goes, but we do keep a check all the time to see that it does not go below the floor. The floor is established in that way.
The same practice is followed in connection with hogs and bacon. We know the relationship between A hogs and bacon and B hogs and bacon. We check all markets to see that the floor price under hogs is maintained. We do not raise any complaint if the price is higher than the floor, but if it gets down close to the floor price we draw the attention of those who are operating on the market to the fact that they are drawing close to the floor and we insist on their not going below the floor. As I have said on one or two occasions before, the only record we have of prices going below what would be justified by the floor prices was during some of the strikes that occurred in the plants during the years these contracts have been in existence.

I should like to say a word or two on the question raised because it has been brought up two or three times, and I think hon. members should understand the position. Everyone who knows the situation in the Lethbridge area sympathizes with those who are running feed lots. The feed lot idea was introduced some years ago to deal with a situation which then existed. In the fall of the year, in September and October, cattle were taken off the grass in great numbers and found their way into the Calgary and Winnipeg markets in such large numbers that they could not be taken care of by the packing houses, so a number of men in Alberta were encouraged to go into the feed lot business, and they bought these cattle either from the farmers or at the Calgary yards and took them to the feed lots and fed them until the spring. That spread the delivery of the cattle over two periods, the fall and the spring, and so helped the farmers in general. That was in a period when there was not a market for all the cattle that were coming on the Winnipeg and Calgary -markets in the fall, and when duties were high on shipments to the United States, so there was nothing to be gained thereby. These men running the feed lots bought the cattle at a price one and a half to two cents lower than the price would be in the spring. That was no great help to the farmer generally, because 90 per cent of

Agricultural Products Act
the farmers are producing not more than twenty head of cattle, and many not more than five or six head. The cattle brought in during the fall were sold at a low price, because there was no ready market for them and these feed lots took them and fed them through until the spring.
Then the war came. Since we have been in the war there has been a market for these cattle every day of the year, and there is no necessity for the farmers taking one and a half to two cents less in the fall in order that somebody may feed them through the winter and make a profit in the spring. From 1942 down to the present the feed1 lots have been having a really difficult problem. It may be argued that probably somebody ought to be dloing something to help, as the opportunity comes, but it should not be the farmer who can now sell his cattle at the market price. He should not take less for them in the fall than he can get for them. I do not know just how we can deal with that problem. It concerns a very small proportion of our beef. Nevertheless these men got into the business through the policy established in Alberta and agreed upon by everybody at that time, but I dio not think it should be done by trying to assure them a price one and a half to two cents Lower than the market price in the fall so that they can feed them through until the spring. We will give more study to the question and see if there is any way of dealing with the problem.

Even now could the minister not dio something to help these people by allowing them to send their beef across the line? If it is only a localized problem, perhaps they could be given a special opportunity to ship their beef across the line. I do not see any reason why the excellent facilities for producing beef in that area should be destroyed. About 40,000 beef are being fed there, and that is no small consideration in any nation. We have every facility there for feeding, an abundance of hay and a territory abounding in feed. Every opportunity is there for producing beef. Why should we destroy those facilities?
There is just one thing the minister did not mention in his statement which was otherwise quite clear. These beef producers take feeder cattle that are not priced as high as the cattle which are more or less finished and which the packers are ready to buy. There is need in this country for somebody to take feeder cattle and support the price by feeding them in the feed lots. It is just because of the need of having support for feeder cattle that this matter becomes of such
importance to the range man who is producing beef out on the hills. If he does not have feeders to buy his semi-finished feeder cattle in the fall he will have to accept a reduced price for his cattle, and it is of importance to the farmer who, as the minister said, produces only five or six cattle that the feeder be there to support prices. The minister agrees with that, I am sure, and so I plead with him that something be done to prevent this excellent facility from being destroyed.
We are in an irrigated area; we are in an area which produces a great deal of sugar. In the production of that sugar there is a great deal of by-products of the sugar factories. Among these are beet pulp and beet molasses, which are exceedingly valuable for feeding. Because the producers are in an irrigated area, they must have crop rotation. Because of that, there is a great deal of hay produced. Hay production is an important industry for a great many people in that area. In addition to that they require the fertilization which comes naturally from feeding stock. All these elements are found in that area. Provision should be made for their use for the benefit of Canada.
If the beef feeder goes out of the picture; if the stock feeder generally in the wintertime goes out of the picture, a serious disadvantage will be created there for a number of people besides the range producer of beef. Once more may I urge that the minister do something about this matter because it is now quite serious. It is costing these men in the neighbourhood of seventy cents a day to feed a steer. That means it is costing them about thirty-five cents a pound to put on the weight now. If they have to go on for a number of days producing beef at thirty-five cents a pound, as they are at present, and they have to sell that beef at 16i cents or 16J cents, then the loss they will sustain will be serious.

In view of the short discussion we have had here, I think I should take two or three minutes to state our position. It was made very clear in the resolution stage of this measure. These are the words I used. Our general position on this measure is known. We are opposed to it in principle; we are opposed to it because it is a complete negation of the form of farm marketing act which we favour, and which our producers are seeking from one end of this country to the other. We favour an act based on the principle of provincially sponsored marketing boards operated by the organized farmers themselves. We favour legislation which gives the producers themselves more say in the fixing of the prices of their products than is allowed in this measure.
The government's program with respect to agricultural prices is expressed effectively in two measures, the Canadian Wheat Board Act under which the wheat contract with Britain is administered, and this Agricultural Products Act under which these contracts with Britain for beef, bacon and cheese and eggs and so on are made and administered. I stated briefly our position with respect to the former act a few days ago. I can state as briefly our position with respect to this one now in words somewhat similar.
The purpose of the original Natural Products Marketing Act, 1934, was to market the farmers' crops to the best advantage as regards total price, stability of payments and orderly marketing. But the government is now following a policy to serve another end. It is using this measure as a price control mechanism more than as an agricultural marketing board; and for that purpose it has sold in the past, and no doubt will sell in the future, farmers' products at less than those farmers could get for their products if sold by themselves. Instead of a price supporting agency, as the original Natural Products Marketing Act was intended to be, and was, the government is using the present measure as a price depressing agency in its plans to regulate price controls or price levels in this country. That is a complete perversion of the original conception of the Natural Pro-

National Film. Board,
ducts Marketing Act. On that ground we opposed this measure in the resolution stage and for the same reasons we oppose it at this time.
Mr. GARDINER moved the third reading of the bill.
