The house resumed at eight o'clock. SUPPLY
Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee of supply.

Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, there is a matter I should like to raise because it is one of some importance to both our own country and others. With your permission I shall introduce what I intend to say by reading a Canadian Press dispatch from Sydney, Australia, under date of March 8, 1948:
The recent decision to close the Canadian national film board offices in Sydney and Melbourne is regarded by film societies throughout Australia as a serious setback to the cultural development of the country.
Almost daily, educational authorities are writing letters to leading newspapers expressing appreciation of the work done by the board since the offices were opened and deploring the severance of a valuable link between Canada and Australia.
Typical of the letters is one from C. N. M. Richmond, president of the Canberra film centre, in today's Sydney Morning Herald. Richmond stressed his disappointment that the board was closing its offices and continued: "In the past two years nearly one third of all films on the programs of the Canberra film centre have been Canadian film board productions and this high proportion is no accident, for the admirable quality of most films from this source now is generally acknowledged.
But there is a further point that the Canadian film board has developed a tradition which had already helped our own national film board- through the work of men like Ralph Foster and Stanley Hawes-so that apart from the film supply we can ill afford to lose Miss Helen Watson and her office as a direct link with the outstanding film work of cur sister dominion."
Richmond concludes with the query: "Is it too late for the Canadian film board to think again and leave at least its Sydney office intact?"
The dispatch says:
Miss Watson closes the Australian offices March 31.
Then it goes on to say this:
It is estimated that almost one million five hundred thousand Australians saw Canadian documentary and non-theatrical films last year. The board's library of more than 300 film subjects was screened 16,400 times in Australia during the year.
In Ottawa Ross McLean, federal government film commissioner, said the national film board had been obliged to indicate the closing of its office in Australia "on the grounds of economy".
"But other ways to make Canadian films available in Australia are being studied," he concluded.
This is not the whole story. We look at the estimates and find that they have been cut by $202,000

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: By approximately ten per cent.

-which is approximately ten per cent. But may I remind the minister that a cut of ten per cent for an organization of this description, with the increase in the price of supplies, means a loss of considerably more than ten per cent to the work of the national film board. As I understand it, the other offices of the film board in the United States and in the United Kingdom, if they are not closed down, will be cut down and their activities greatly restricted. As I say, the estimates which have been tabled in the house recently indicate a sharp cut-for that is what it amounts to-in the film board estimates. I believe that this will not only lead to a curtailment of the excellent overseas work that is being done but also a curtailment of the work in the domestic field. Those of us who come from rural districts in Canada know well how splendidly the national film board has been serving the rural communities; and, after all, those communities are entitled to consideration from this house. I do not like the description that is sometimes applied to some of these films, when they are called movies. These days movies have a connotation that is sometimes not flattering. The national film board products are something more than movies. They are educational films building up good will among all our people all across this country and across the world. From my observation I say that this organization has done a great deal in building up a varied, efficient and interesting rural life and in assisting our educational institutions in those areas. Last year's cut, for there was a cut last year-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
A negligible cut.
National Film Board
-reduced the circuits; or something reduced the circuits. I see that the minister shakes his head.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A negligible cut.

But the costs went up; and as I say, with the higher costs, even a negligible cut in the estimates means more than a negligible cut in the work. In any event, last year's cut reduced the circuits from eighty-five to sixty-seven, and we are told that these are economy measures. There are places where we can economize, but there are others where it is false economy to cut and I believe that this is one of them. The curtailment of the national film board's activities at home and abroad is, I believe, a penny-wise, pound-foolish policy. Relentless cutting is never wholly an economy measure, because we sometimes cut and find that, instead of economizing, we are less efficient; and that is not economy. The Department of National Revenue is, of course, responsible for the film board's activities. It seems to me that the estimates indicate that the cut is an arbitrary one without very much consideration as to what the consequences will be. The argument that is used, namely, that the development of the film board was an abnormal outgrowth of wartime activity, I do not think can be properly substantiated. Indeed, had there been no war, it seems to me that these services would have been developed. Now, when we need to unify our people in peacetime I am of the opinion that the film board's activities should continue to be developed and should enjoy a natural growth from the point at which we are now, not from the point at which we were before the war. I should not like to think it is the intention of the government or of the minister in charge consciously to cripple the potentialities for good of the national film board. But if the government intends to cut down or to eliminate the activities of the national film board, I think it is a matter that should be discussed in the house and the government should frankly tell us exactly what its attitude is.
This is one of several matters upon which this house has been negligent. We have never made a proper appraisal of the work of the national film board. We have never had an objective assessment of its activities as we have, for example, of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and when it has been raised in the house from time to time it has been kicked around something like a political football.
For years, for example, my hon. friend the member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser)

has criticized the film board. I wonder if the hon. member has done what some of the rest of us have done-visited the film board, seen what it is doing, and looked over the work that is being done under terrific difficulties in the seven scattered buildings in this city.
Twelve.
Has the hon. member visited those twelve buildings?
You have six more to see, then.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Seven from twelve is five.

Yes, five. The hon. member said that the Minister of Public AVorks (Mr. Fournier) should take note of the condition of some of these buildings in which the film board employees are doing the best they can. The conditions are really a disgrace to the government of Canada; for example, the conditions under which some of the people are working on what is called the island. Those conditions are unbelievable; and if a private organization were using such buildings and keeping employees engaged in them under similar conditions, the government of Ontario, under the factory act or a measure of that kind, would step in and compel the employer to put the place in proper condition to be occupied.
Not even a good factoiy.

I suggest that before hon. members make a criticism of the work of an institution, whether it be one of our own institutions or any other, at least some careful inquiry should be made into what is being [DOT]there carried on. I understand that the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) has visited the film board buildings in this city. Apparently he is unavoidably absent tonight. I am sorry he is not here, because I should like to have heard what the hon. gentleman has to say. I should like to hear the hon. member who sits to my immediate right, the member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol), who has taken a considerable interest in what the film board employees are doing. I believe he could speak with some authority on the achievements of the board.
As I said a few moments ago, recently I took a look around to see under what conditions the film board employees were operating in this city, and apart from the utterly appalling conditions in which those employees are compelled to work, I think the board is something in which all Canadians can take considerable pride. I believe they are doing a

National Film Board
splendid job. I have before me an editorial from the Moving Picture Digest dated March 13, 1948. This magazine normally speaks for private enterprise and, therefore, would not be considered to be particularly interested in a government institution of this kind; but what does this moving picture digest say? Under the title. ''Why publicly spank the baby?" it reminds us that the film board is a creature of this parliament and it asks why the baby must always be subjected to public spankings. It refers to "Canada Carries On," which many of us have seen in the theatres week by week, as being a first class production, ns indeed it is recognized to be by film authorities in the United States and elsewhere. It praises the film board's record and concludes with this statement:
An investigation, by competent men, to save operation costs is a reasonable business consideration. blit why not investigate, get the facts, get the figures before we blast and publicly spank our baby?
And the costs too.
And t/he costs as well.
I have been there.

That is what I mean. Let us investigate before we come to a decision condemning something which I think is doing a good job for Canada.
In my investigation of what the national film board was doing I found that there is very careful treasury control of all the expenditures undertaken by the film board and its staff-an internal audit, treasury board audit -and if there is a treasury audit, our experience in this house must indicate that the treasury is pretty tight when it comes to the expenditure of public money.
The film board was first established early in 1939 as an agency to correlate all government film activities. There were a number of activities before that time; but this was the first time they were correlated under one board, and its purpose was and is to provide films interpreting Canada on much broader films than travelling industrial productions could possibly do such as heretofore have made up the bulk of the government's film programs.
May I emphasize, contrary to what is sometimes said, that the national film board was not a wartime creation? Today the national film board remains on a broader scale and I think the reasons are obvious why it should function on a broader scale. Over the last nine years, Canada's own demands created all kinds of services which the film board had to undertake; hence the expansion of the capacities and functions of the organization as
the times demanded. Under wartime conditions, as we all know, and as I 'have said before, Canada developed a documentary film organization that is first class. I was going to say unsurpassed, but it 'is first class and has often been compared with the excellent documentary films that are produced in the United Kingdom. Let me suggest that, before we agree to the drastic cutting of estimates for this organization, we should measure the film board's achievements, and we should measure them by the yardstick of merit.
Some people say, of course, that it has expanded its activities. So it has. But in my opinion the expansion of those activities is something to be commended and not deplored, and if merit is to be the standard of judgment, then I say that we shall find that the organization ranks high.
I should say, in addition, that the documentary films of the board are regarded in other countries as models to be followed; and, as we learn and know, inquiries regarding these documentary films flow in constantly from all over the world-Mexico, South Africa, Australia, Sweden, the British isles and elsewhere. And as I have indicated, by press dispatch, the threatened closing of the office in Australia is causing considerable consternation.
Among whom?

Among people who are interested in educational films in Australia. We know the pattern of the national film board has been followed very closely by the Australian government itself. A Canadian, a member of the national film board staff, was the first commissioner of the Australian film organization.
On March 10 there were tabled and distributed to hon. members facts concerning this organization's activities. I hope they will be studied by all hon. members. Anyone looking them over will find that every year thousands of prints go out from the film board for domestic and foreign use. Some are, of course, sold to commercial concerns, and they bring in some small revenue. However I was there the other day and saw their library and, of photographs alone, I am told they have approximately 80,000 negatives of various types, other than the actual war types. These are all indexed and contain a full history of our country' during the time the national film board has operated.
In addition to those supplied to commercial organizations, thousands of others are rented for use by various non-commercial bodies. The figures which are given in the
National Film Board

report-and they are quite impressive-did not include prints of newsreel stories, of which sixteen were released by major newsreel companies in the United States for world distribution, reaching audiences estimated at more than 70,000,000. That is one kind of release which reaches an audience of 70,000,000 people, advertising our country and interpreting various phases of Canadian life abroad. Today Canada has the largest non-theatrical showings of any country in the world; and this, it seems to me, suggests that the use of films should be encouraged as an effective means of increasing the free flow of information, not only in our country but throughout the world.
And may I ask, Mr. Speaker, if there ever was a time in the world's history when that free flow of information was needed more badly then it is at the present time? If one picks up this evening's paper he will read of the discussions going on now at Geneva regarding the free flow of information.
Here we have an organization which is giving information all across the world about our country, interpreting us to them and them to us. The appalling ignorance of one country about another leads to all kinds of misunderstandings. If we knew more about each other I am convinced that the preservation of peace would not be nearly as difficult as it is now. The iron curtain which keeps us from knowing what is going on behind it, and keeps the people behind it from knowing what we are doing is one of the greatest dangers in the world today. Anything that tends to bring information to people across the world is a most valuable asset to any country. If the people of Russia and those of the western world were able to learn more about each other's problems I am convinced we would find it easier to reach satisfactory understandings.
But while this lack of understanding is greatly to be deplored, in my view even more deplorable is the ignorance of free peoples about one another. Any of us who have travelled' know perfectly well how appallingly ignorant people in other countries are about Canada. I am sure that every Canadian serviceman-I have heard them say so and, having visited the old land several times, I can confirm it-was shocked at the lack of knowledge about Canada to be found in the British isles.
They are still ignorant of this country.

And exactly the same thing would apply here, perhaps in various parts of the country. Certainly in the United

States there is appalling ignorance of Canada, and perhaps among some of our own people just as great a degree of ignorance of the United States.
That ignorance extends to all peoples everywhere. Anything that can break down that barrier and bring about better information and better understanding should be supported. As has been said so often in the house, today we face the threat of a new tyranny. In the final analysis, the only way to overcome that tyranny is more information, more education and more understanding among the common people of the world; for the common people do not want misunderstanding; they do not want war. The common people are the ones who suffer most when war comes.
I think it is wrong, then, to reduce these estimates. It is wrong to cut out services we have rendered1 to our sister communities of the British commonwealth and to Great Britain. Today in many countries-in Australia, for example-there is a paper shortage. The same applies in Great Britain, with the result that if you wish to interpret your life and conditions to that other country you cannot do so on paper. Then, if you wish to use some other medium, certainly one of the best available is films, because perhaps we learn more through the eye than we do in any other way.
I would like to see Canada set up a UNESCO commission in our own country, and make available all the facilities for proper representation at its conferences. But at the present time we are cutting out one of the chief instruments of education and information at our disposal.
True, perhaps we must economize. But let us economize in places where we can do so and' not exercise a false economy. Let me illustrate in this way. Last year's exhibition allotment of the Department of Trade and Commerce for the commonwealth exhibition in Sydney, Australia, cost- the country $10,000. That was for only a short time. Many people would walk by it casually, as we do at exhibitions, but only a fraction of them would really look at what was demonstrated' there. Now we propose to cut out the office of the film board at Sydney, Australia, which performs all the functions I outlined at the beginning of my observations. The salaries in the Australian film board offices were $7,500. The total outlay for the office was a little over $10,000. The job done by the film board in Australia was done for 365 days of the year, and was carried out into the most remote places of our sister dominion. Just as they go into the remote places of our sister dominion, so

National Film Board
do film board: films go into the remote places in our own country, and bring education and entertainment to our own people.

Do any films come from
Australia? Do they reciprocate?

We happen to be ahead of them in this matter. However, I have no doubt that under the leadership of a Canadian, who was on the film board, they will be producing documentary films we shall have an opportunity to enjoy.
During the war they had some.

Yes, during the war they had. I was going to say that one of the most interesting full-length films made recently, one which I believe received an award, is an Australian film the title of which now escapes me, but which, I believe, shows the driving of the herds across the great continent of Australia. I say that the expansion, which has been quite fast, should not be retarded; that we should give every encouragement to this group of people who are doing such an excellent job.
Of course there is bound to be a limit.
If the hon. member for New Westminster who keeps interrupting me will just be patient he can say whatever he wants to say later on. I know there must be a limit.
You remember that when I am speaking and do not interrupt me.

I do not interrupt the hon. gentleman. The hon. gentleman has been interrupting me almost continuously. I am quite willing to answer a question, and if an hon. gentleman who does not agree with me will rise in his place and ask a question I will sit down and then get up and answer it, but I object to having a running fire of interruptions with hon. members sitting in their seats.
I will watch you when you are speaking and you will not get away with it next time.

Instead of cutting down, I say that we should be expanding the service by intelligent degrees. It is senseless to cut down arbitrarily the work of this organization as the estimate implies will be done. I want to make two pleas to the government. First, the cut should be reconsidered and I think there is enough evidence to show that it should be reconsidered. Second, an opportunity should be provided for fuller consideration of the work of this organization than has been provided heretofore. I think hon. members have
a right to ask the film board authorities to appear before a parliamentary committee so that they can get all the facts. The hon. member for New Westminster or the hon. member for Peterborough West-
Leave me out.
-who has indicated that money has been wastefully used and that this organization is not worthwhile-
I should like to correct the hon. gentleman. I have not at any time said that the film board was not worthwhile.

I am glad to hear that. I misunderstood the purport of the hon. gentleman's questions. That would give him an opportunity to inquire into all the features which he thinks should be inquired into and it would give the rest of us an understanding of what this organization is doing. Just as we set up a committee to inquire into the work of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, so we should set up a committee to inquire into the work of the national film board. If that is done we should all be in a better position to form a considered judgment. I suggest that two things be done: that the present cut in the estimates should be reconsidered and that, after we come back following the Easter recess, there should be set up a committee before which the officers of the film board could appear and which would give us an opportunity of inquiring into all the phases of the work of this organization.

Mr. Speaker, I know that you are not anxious to sit in the chair much longer, that you want to get down to this other work, but I do not believe it would be fair if I did not have an opportunity to say a few words. I am pleased that the hon. gentleman has brought up this matter this evening, although if I had had an opportunity to go up to my office I might have been better prepared to reply. The hon. member started off by mentioning the fact that the Sydney, Australia, office had been closed.
As I understand the purpose of the setting up of the film board in 1939, it was that it would buy or make films for the different departments of the government and for educational purposes. I have a brief here outlining the whole set-up but I have not had a chance to go through it since the hon. member began to speak. I believe I am right in saying that the Department of Trade and Commerce was to distribute these films in the different countries, not the national film board. The film board was only to produce the films for the
National Film, Board

different departments. The Department of Trade and Commerce, having a full understanding of the different countries, could pick out the proper pictures to be distributed in those countries through its trade offices.
Mention was made in the article read by the hon. member that the Australian film board was sorry that the national film board was closing its office in Australia. No doubt that is true. I do not blame the Australian film board for feeling that way because, by the national film board being in Australia, the Australian film board was saved thousands and thousands of dollars in distribution costs. There is no doubt of that. Not only did we supply them with films made by the film board, I have no doubt that we supplied them with other films made by commercial firms. I hope that most of the films distributed in Australia were made by commercial firms and I will tell you why in a few moments.
I feel as the hon. member does, and as I think every hon. member does, that every agency of government should be used to build up good will in other countries. I have preached that in the house on many occasions. I even suggested that the former minister of trade and commerce should take a trip to South and Central America. He did.
Oh, oh.

The hon. member for
Hamilton East laughs. He evidently feels that the minister's trip was of no use, but I feel that it was of some use. The hon. member is a Liberal member and, of course, you could not expect anything else.
He is not even an independent.

No, he is not even an independent. The hon. member who has just taken his seat said that he had visited the film board. I have visited it on different occasions right from 1940. I did not wait until the last couple of years to visit it. On Saturday morning I was over at 71 Bank street on an invitation from the film board to see some films they were showing. They sent out invitations to a program starting at eleven o'clock and running until twelve thirty. I got a special invitation from the secretary of the film board, and I suppose I was the only one who did. However I was going anyhow. I have spoken to some of our own members and none of them got it. Two other members and another party went with me. There were four Progressive Conservatives and two Liberals in a theatre seating fifty people. The film board showed, first of all, what they call "Eyewitness-First Shots of

Chalk River". That was a fairly good picture, but of course they could not show very much of the Chalk River plant.
Then they showed "Trade Mission to South Africa". That included a picture of the former minister of trade and commerce-
Good.

I believe even the hon. member for Hamilton East could take a better picture than was made by the member of the national film board who took that picture. It looked to me as if it had been taken by the rankest amateur. It was really a poor picture. The person who took it had evidently very little knowledge of taking pictures in southern countries. A person going into a southern country where the light is extremely strong must find out from people who are taking pictures there just how the lighting should be, what filters to use and how they should be used. That picture was an absolute flop. What it cost the taxpayers I do not know.
They had another picture "Great Lakes". It was supposed to be in colour. It wras on colour film.
A good picture too.

That shows that the hon. gentleman does not know a good picture from a bad one. It showed a picture of Windsor, and I will acknowledge that some of the shots were good but the picture as a whole was extremely poor. The colour picture was taken when the light was very strong. I think it was taken at noon because the shadows showed straight up and down. Those who are taking colour pictures, unless they know exactly what filters to use, should take them in the morning before the sun is too strong, or in the evening just when the sun is setting, to get the best results.
No excuse for not getting a good picture of a beautiful city like Windsor.

They also showed a film "Farm Homes Beautiful". That is a picture, Mr. Speaker, that is really worthwhile. The photography in it was not up to what it should be, not as good as it would have been if taken by a commercial firm, but it was such an improvement on the other pictures that it really looked good to me. It is a picture that I feel should be shown in the rural sections of Canada, instead of some of those other pictures they are sending out. They sent out a picture in my district on "Soil", to a section of the country which can grow only rock, where there is no farming at all. Even a member

National Film Board
of the federation of agriculture said about that picture, "I was absolutely disgusted when they threw it on the screen."
On Saturday they showed another picture
West Wind", in the Canadian Artists series
Tom Thomson-filmed in Algonquin park. I am not prejudiced; that is an Ontario picture. It was really an excellent picture; but it was taken, not by the national film board, but by Crawley Films. The colour in it just stood out. You could see it was in perfect colour. Every detail in it was perfect, not like the other pictures, blurred and hard on your eyes, but a real picture that you could look at a second time, a picture you would be proud of.
The hon. member mentioned the buildings the film board occupies. He said seven buildings. There are twelve, ten of them rented buildings and two owned by the government. I have a return which shows that is a fact. I do not want to say anything against the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann), *who looks after the national film board, and who signed this return, so it must be true. I will acknowledge that practically every government building needs cleaning and repairing. I think the minister who is in charge of public works will acknowledge that too, and I hope that as soon as times are better and building materials a little cheaper, and men available to do the work, the necessary cleaning and repairs will be done to these government buildings. But personally I feel that veterans homes must come first. I hope we shall do as much for them as possible and leave this other work until later. It is not only here in Ottawa where government buildings need repair but in practically every city in Canada. If you travel in the United States you will find the same conditions there. The hon. member who mentioned seven buildings may have got that figure from an editorial in one of the papers which mentioned seven buildings and incidentally tried to pan me. At the present time the film board is spending over one and a half million dollars on salaries out of a budget of about $2,200,000, and on top of that there are travelling expenses; I have not those expenses here, but they are in Hansard and show over $300,000.
Last year I was invited to visit the film board and I would have gone but at the time committees of the house were sitting and the house was also sitting in the morning, I believe.
I tried five telephones to get hold of this party to tell him I would prefer having the appointment moved forward, but I could not raise anybody until a quarter to ten o'clock. I did
not try all the 132 telephones which the film board has; I tried only five.
I do not want anybody to believe or think I am not in favour of films for educational purposes, and films to advertise Canada in eveiy part of the world. The proper films can do a wonderful job, but those films must be distributed in other countries, not by 'the film board, which does not know a thing about distributing films to the right people in foreign countries, but by the trade and commerce department, which knows every angle of the business and knows what the people want.
There is no better medium of education than films of the right kind. The children love them and so do the children who have grown up to the age of you and me; but we love good pictures, not some of these fuzzy pictures that the film board puts out. I know that in rural districts films have done an excellent job. They have done an excellent job in agriculture; but, Mr. Speaker, do you think they can do a decent job with agriculture if they do not have a little direction from the Minister of Agriculture and his department? The federation of agriculture have also asked for motion pictures. With the proper films, agriculture in Canada will improve and find out the different ways and means of doing its job. It is an excellent way to show the farmers of the country the proper way to look after their soil, their crops, and insect control, and the more pictures we have of that kind the better, but we must have people taking these pictures who understand how to take them and what kind of pictures to take.
I understand that in the United' States the government of that country have all their films made and processed by commercial companies. I might be wrong in that, but I do not think I am, as I have had a great number of letters from people who are in the film business, despite the paper read by the hon. member, saying, "Go to it; you are on the right track." The first week after I spoke in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne-that was February 25-I had 216 letters from photographers throughout Canada saying that they were having unfair competition from the national film board in their photographic business. As taxpayers, they felt that they should not be taxed to pay for unfair competition in their own line of business.
Last year the national film board got out a catalogue, "Canada 1947-48". It is a wonderful catalogue; it has beautiful pictures in it; they are Canadian subjects. These pictures are sold right across Canada in competition with
National Film Board

their own photographers. That is one department of the national film board which should be closed down.
The film board asked the architectural association-I think that is the proper name for it -to send in all their photographs of public buildings and to be sure to have them copyrighted so that the national film board would have all right to them; and even the photographers who took them would not have any say as to w'here they went or get any benefit from them.
During the last week I have had a number of telephone calls; I have also had people come in to see me, and I heard something that almost makes me wonder what this country of ours is coming to. I believe there is a place around Ottawa called Fairy lake park; I am not sure that that is the proper name for it. A gentleman was there taking some pictures, and he was plump and plainly told by the national film board man who was there with a camera that he had no business taking pictures on that property because it belonged to the federal government. I have also had commercial photographers tell me that they have been told to keep off the grounds in front of this building because it was government property and that they were not to take pictures there; that it was the right and the sole right of the national film board to take pictures on federal property. I can hardly believe that, but these men are, I know, responsible men and I feel quite sure that they would not say anything that was not true.
I hold in my hand a return which shows the most outlandish picture I have seen in a long time. It is a Christmas card; it has "N.F.B." on one corner and "O.N.F." on the other. Inside the cover it says, "The film commissioner and staff of the national film board wish you a merry Christmas and a happy New Year." That is paid for by the taxpayers of Canada.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The initials to which the hon. member refers probably means the national film board in French.

That may be so; my French is not as good this year as it was last year.
_ I have enough material here, Mr. Speaker, to talk on the national film board until two o'clock in the morning-
Don't bother.

-and I think I could give you something new every minute. I do not know who gave permission to the national film board to come here on March 16 and take a still picture, to set their camera over on the other side and take a picture across this way.

They took a picture of the Hansard reporters; but over on this side, standing away to the left of me-
Where all the smart people are.

An hon. member says,
"Where all the smart people are". He is perfectly right. It was the messengers of the House of Commons and other members of the staff of the house who sat there while that picture was being taken. I agree with him that they are very smart and pleasant fellows with whom to deal. I like all the messengers here, but I do not think a picture of that kind should be taken in the House of Commons with a set-up of that kind. I do not think it is right, because what they will have to do is either to blur out the faces of the messengers and the staff or put the heads of some members of parliament on their bodies-
That will weaken the messengers.

I want to say again, as I said to the hon. member who spoke before me,
I have never said at any time that the national film board should be done away with. I have said that the national film board should have a clean-up. The national film board should do what it was set up to do in 1939 when it had a budget of only $80,000. I have always said that the national film board could do good work if it had the proper guidance.
An hon. member says that the treasury board checks all the vouchers and things. That may be so, Mr. Speaker, but what do the treasury board know about films? They know figures, yes; they know what a dollar is, yes; but they do not know the workings of the national film board; and when a voucher comes through, if it is signed by an officer of the film board it will be approved and passed. Despite what any editorial says, or what anyone else might say, the sooner the national film board has a mopping-up, a clean-up and proper direction, the better for this Canada of ours, and the better trade relations we shall have with the other countries because they will appreciate good pictures after the bad national film board pictures they have been having.
farmers' income tax

I rise at this time, Mr. Speaker, to bring before the house a matter which I think is now of the utmost importance to the farmers of Canada, namely, the farmers' income tax. Protests are coming in from western Canada by the hundreds. Never before have I received as many

Farmers' Income Tax
letters from my constituency on any single subject as I am now receiving with respect to farmers' income tax. The farmers feel so strongly on this particular matter that many protest meetings are being held. These meetings are spontaneous; they are not organized by any person touring the country. The farmers in a given locality feel that they have a just complaint and they meet together in considerable numbers to send their protests to members of parliament and to the government. Just recently a large meeting was held in the city of Swift Current, during bad weather, at which 148 farmers attended and as a result of which protests were sent to the members of parliament and to the government. The hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bentley) and other members of this party go along with me in protesting the type of income tax form and the method used in making the farmers comply with it. In one town of my constituency the farmers have formed a farmers' income tax association; two hundred farmers around one small prairie town have formed themselves into an income tax association. Another town has farmers who are organizing a widespread campaign to send in petitions against the present income tax form.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Is the hon. member seriously contending now that the announcement made by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) last Friday is not satisfactory?

Yes, I contend that. I shall come to that particular point a little later on.
The records show, Mr. Speaker, that in the past the farmers of western Canada have more than paid their share of the income taxes which have been paid by farmers from one end of Canada to the other. Just a few days ago Chester A. Bloom, writing in the Free Press, gave the figures with regard to income tax paid in 1945-46 by farmers in the various provinces. In that year the farmers in Quebec paid total income taxes of $59,900; the farmers in Ontario paid a little over $1,000,000 in taxes; the farmers in Saskatchewan paid more than $2,500,000; the farmers in Manitoba paid more than $1,800,000, and the farmers in Alberta paid more than $1,100,000.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

Did the hon. member consider the fact that the income of the western
farmer is much higher than the average income of the farmer in the province of Quebec?
So are their expenses.

That is perhaps a point, but I think the hon. member should also know the number of farmers in the provinces. For example, in 1945 Ontario had 175,749 farmers; Quebec, 151,850; Saskatchewan, 138,370. There are a great many more farmers in Ontario and Quebec than there are in Saskatchewan.
Does the hon. member contend that it is a question of the number of farmers or is it not a question of the amount of income of the individual farmer?
I think it is a question of both.
I do not think so.
I think it is a question of both. I do not think the hon. member will contend that in Quebec, for example, every farmer who should have paid income tax has, in fact, done so.
Oh, yes, they have.
No, he does contend that; and I do not contend that for Saskatchewan.
I imagine so.

All I am trying to point out is that the farmers of Saskatchewan have paid what I consider to be a reasonable share of the income tax paid by farmers in Canada as a whole. More than that, there is a concerted drive on in western Canada at the present time to get farmers to file returns whether they have filed them before or not. Most farmers find it impossible to keep an adequate set of accounts. Certainly they cannot remember all the expenses they had, for example, in 1944. Therefore, when they are making returns now they must pretty much guess at the figures. More than that, I think the government is requiring a good deal of unnecessary work and worry over the filing of these returns on the part of many farmers who certainly will not be paying any income tax at all; for in my opinion a farmer on a small farm cannot, over a period of three years, earn sufficient income to warrant his paying any tax.
One of the major complaints of farmers in respect of income tax is that, during the whole of the nineteen-thirties, their debts accumulated drastically, but it was not until 1943 that prices of farm products improved to any extent. Moreover, in 1942 there was a rigid quota against wheat, also in 1943. Then
Farmers' Income Tax

in 1944 farmers had an opportunity to market much of their 1942 and 1943 crops along with their 1944 crop. No consideration has been given to the fact that within one year a farmer marketed parts at least of three crops. Moreover, if a farmer paid; $1 to reduce his indebtedness, that $1 was subject to income tax. It was considered! income for taxation purposes. So the farmers feel that they are not being given fair and just treatment. Today in many instances they find! that they have replaced a debt owed to a mortgage company by a debt owed to the federal Department of National Revenue. I shall quote part of a letter which was sent to me. I picked out this ome at random from those I received, and I think it fairly well states the position of the farmers of western Canada in this regard. It reads in part as follows:
For years the loan companies bled us white and just when we are getting on our feet after ten years of drought, the government steps in to put us back where we were before. What I would like to know is, what right has the government to hold this money indefinitely-
Meaning the wheat board participation certificates.
-without paying us interest; yet if the farmer owes them back income tax, they hook him for a 5 per cent penalty?
That is a good question that has not been answered. The farmers are being forced to pay a good deal of income tax at the present time; still the government says it wants livestock production. Farmers are not producing livestock because they find it is of little benefit, since a good part of the income they make from extra work producing livestock goes not to themselves but to the federal income tax department.
The government got out what it called a simplified form, and along with that form went a book of instructions. I think it is good that farmers were given this book of instructions. It will be of some benefit to them, and certainly items whereby farmers can write down their various receipts and expenditures are a good thing. But it seems to me that a good part of the introductory portion of the farmers' income tax guide is devoted to propaganda.
There is one question: "What are the things Canadians get through their government? What are we paying for?" The answer is this: "We are paying for the after-cost of our part in the winning of two world wars, which, had we lost, would have plunged us into the terrors, the deprivations, the serfdom and the hopelessness which afflict the majority of the people in the world today."
The farmers' income tax guide goes on to say: "We are paying for social services." This

is what the money is going for: old age pensions, and family allowances ini particular, but also health services and many other benefits.
I do not know who gets health services from the federal government when he is ill. I do not know if this was written in the hope that health services would be provided by the federal government, but certainly I do not think it is a statement of fact to say that the federal government is spending money for health services. The simplified form makes it necessary, I believe, for the farmer to hire an accountant to keep his books throughout the year and then hire a lawyer to fill in the income tax form at the end of the year. And the government, in forcing all farmers, whether they are liable or not, to file forms is creating some employment. It is creating jobs for the lawyers and the real estate agents and what have you. But in my opinion it involves a lot of wasted time and a lot of money spent by the farmers, many of whom should not, in my opinion, come within the income tax regulations at all.
The minister announced that some changes were made in regard to the net worth section of the farmers' simplified form. I do not think the announcement meets the situation. On March 19, as reported at page 2400 of Hansard, the minister said:
The department therefore has decided that (a) those farmers who report their income for 1947 on a cash basis need not complete the farmer's net worth statement section of the return. There may be individual cases where, after the filing of the return, the department will require from a farmer, as from any other taxpayer, in order to make a proper assessment of his income, a statement of assets and liabilities of his business, or other additional information which, in such eases, will be requested in the usual manner.
I wonder if the information will include the part of the net worth section which calls for the farmer to disclose the amount of cash he has on his person or on the farm. I do not know and the minister did not say. Then, to conclude the quotation:
(b) Those farmers who report 1947 incomes on an accrual basis must attach to the return a statement of assets and liabilities, as heretofore, or complete the appropriate parts of the net worth statement attached to the return.
Any bona fide farmer in western Canada will file his income tax return on an accrual basis. He is given an opportunity to spread his income over a period of three years, so that he will report his income for taxation purposes on an accrual basis and, if he does that, then he must submit a net worth statement attached to the return. The minister did not state whether that net worth statement which must be at-

Farmers' Income Tax
tached to the return is the same type and has the same parts in it as the net worth section of the 1947 income tax form. If it is, then there is no real change, because of the minister's announcement, for the reason that every man who is in the business of farming will want his income spread over a period of three years.
One of the reasons the farmer will want that done is that he suffers crop failures every now and- then. If I do not miss my guess he will still have to sell his oats, barley and flax on the grain exchange, and these prices will vary a great deal. The farmer's income will fluctuate greatly because of the operation of the grain exchange and because of recurring crop failures; therefore every farmer almost will want to file his income tax return on an accrual basis, and when he does that he must submit the net worth statement.
I contend, therefore, that the minister's announcement has not cleared up the situation in that respect at all. The farmers are asking that their income tax be spread, not over a period of three years only but over a period of five years. Farming is very hazardous. It is particularly hazardous in the prairie provinces. The farmer may get a forty-bushel crop one year and no crop at all for another two years, and because of that the farmers believe that the only fair thing is to have their income tax spread over a period of five years, a moving average for five years, which would be in effect a ten-year average.
They also feel that the present-day exemptions are far too low. They feel that the exemption of a single man to the extent of $750 and a married couple to the extent of $1,500 is ridiculously low. No young man can hope to pay for a farm when, if he earns more than S750, he must pay income tax. The farmers believe that their income tax exemptions should be increased to at least $1,200 for the single man and $2,400 for the married couple.
The farmers are also asking that the principle of the basic herd be extended. Page 17 of the farmers' guide for income tax poses this question: "What is a basic herd and how is it established?" The answer given is this: "Briefly, a basic herd is a capital asset consisting of cattle which have been purchased out of capital or are a replacement of them." The farmers would like the principle of the basic herd applied to all types of livestock found on the farm and not applied only to cattle as at this moment.
I have some figures as to the size of farms in Saskatchewan. I think any hon. member who is familiar with farming in that province will agree that a man who has a half-section of land, or 320 acres, over a period of three
years just cannot earn enough to get into the income tax bracket. I do not think any useful purpose is served) by asking half-section farmers, or smaller, to file income tax returns. Certainly the government will not get any substantial amount of income tax from these farmers. It will create a lot of trouble for them, and they will have to go to a good deal of expense to have the income tax forms filed.
In Saskatchewan in 1946 there were 75,000 farms of 479 acres or less. That is just under three-quarters of a section. The average farmer has one-quarter of a section of land, or two-quarters or three-quarters or more. So that of the 75,000 farmers, I am sure that more than 70,000 have a half-section of land or less. In that province in 1946 there were only 125,000 farmers, so that 60 per cent of the farmers are, I am sure, farming a halfsection of land or less.
Therefore I contend that the government should not ask farmers who are farming that size of farm unit to file income tax returns, because certainly they will not be liable to pay income tax; and by being asked to file income tax returns, they are being asked to go to unnecessary expense.
There are many ways in which present income tax laws should be changed as they affect farmers. The Alberta Farmers' Union and the United Farmers of Canada, Saskatchewan section, have submitted briefs to the government in this respect. They go into a great deal of detail as to the many ways in which farmers' income tax regulations and forms should be changed.
In closing, I should like to outline the nine steps which I consider are most important to correct the present inequities in the income tax regulations as applied to farmers. They are:
1.	Exemptions should be raised to $1,200 for single and $2,400 for married persons.
2.	Payment of arrears of interest and principal due before 1940 should be allowed as deductions for income tax purposes.
3.	The present three-year average should be replaced by a five-year moving average.
4.	There should be simplification of income tax forms and complete abolition of the present net worth section.
5.	Farmers proving investment in land and machinery to a value of less than $10,000 should be exempt from having to file income tax returns, because a farmer with only a $10,000 investment cannot over a period of three years make sufficient money to have to pay income tax.
6.	In case of dispersal sales of livestock a number of animals equivalent to those owned
Farmers' Income Tax

on January 1, 1941, should be considered a capital asset, and not subject to income tax; this to apply to horses, sheep, hogs and poultry, as well as cattle. This is the basic herds clause.
7.	Allowance for labour of farm families in connection with production on the farm should be made.
8.	There should be establishment of a board of arbitration in each province to hear income tax appeals. There is no board in the various provinces now to which the farmers can take their assessments and obtain rulings.
9.	Uniformity of interpretation and administration of the Income Tax Act. It should not be left to the discretion of district inspectors to vary the provisions of the act.
I believe if these changes were made the farmers of Canada, particularly those of western Canada who are willing and anxious to pay their share of income tax, would be in a position to file their returns in a simplified manner, and the government would be able to assess those returns in a more just fashion. It would correct the grave injustices which prevail at the present time.
Carried.

Mr. Speaker, it is not carried yet. I regret having to detain the house for a short time; but I would be remiss in my duty if I failed to take part in this discussion, instituted by the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Argue).
You will be brief, though.

I shall be as brief as I can. I have received so many submissions from people at home complaining about this matter that I feel I must place the weight of their complaints before the house.
When the hon. member for Wood Mountain was speaking, some questions were asked from the other side as to whether he was being fair in pointing out that more pressure was being put upon western farmers for the purpose of collecting income tax from them than is being placed on people in other parts of Canada.
I have here a return given to me by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) in reply to a question I had asked which, I believe, gives some information along that line. According to the 1946 census, there were, in round figures, 270,000 farmers in the three prairie provinces, while in the other provinces there were 436,000, making a total in Canada

of about 705,000. To investigate the farmers of the west, there were 126 inspectors for the 270,000.
What year?

Up to February 19, 1948.
To investigate and inspect the 436,000 farmers in other parts of Canada there were only eighty-eight inspectors. It might be argued that there is more income made in the west, but I am doubtful as to the truth ot that suggestion. The figures I have do not indicate a great deal of difference.
For instance, the Canada Year Book for 1947 gives the 1945 figure, the latest available, of $857,000,000 total farm cash income in the three prairie provinces, whereas in the rest of Canada it was $828,000,000. There is not a great deal of difference in the amount of cash income of the farmers. Nevertheless, in the west there are more inspectors trying to get money from the farmers than there are endeavouring to extract money from farmers in other parts of Canada.
Only a week ago last Friday a meeting was held in my city of Swift Current. Immediately after that meeting I received a wire dated at Swift Current, March 13, stating that a mass meeting had been held in Swift Current that afternoon respecting income tax forms, and stating, "In spite of roads, snow blocked, had 152 in attendance; resolution passed without one dissenting vote." They say they will mail me a copy, which they have done.
I have the minutes of that meeting here. I do not wish to delay the house so that, unless someone forces it, I shall not read these minutes. I have documentary evidence to prove every statement I make and, if requested, I shall take the time of the house to put it on the record, where it cannot be refuted. If the house is willing to take my word for it I shall read only one or two extracts from the proceedings of this meeting. I want to point out that the meeting was comprised of farmers who happened to be in town during a bad stretch of weather when the roads were blocked and when no motor traffic could move outside the city limits. It was called on two days' notice; and only those who could come in by train or had horse transportation, something not plentiful in such a highly mechanized country, were able to get in. They had to hold the meeting in a small hall because we have no civic centre. The skating rink is in use in the wintertime, and that is the place generally used for large meetings. This small hall was crowded with 152 people and there were many more outside who could not take part

Farmers' Income Tax
in the meeting. I might add that everything was quite informal. The letter is addressed to me as "Dear Tom," and they refer to the chairman as "Jim". I quote from the letter:
The meeting was very ably handled by Jim Wightman in the chair and in his opening remarks he prevailed upon those present to forget their party affiliations during this meeting as it was a matter affecting all farmers regardless of their polities, and this in effect was quite evident during the entire meeting as during the lengthy discussion on the resolution members of all political groups were heard from without any mention of party feelings, as all were unanimously in accord with the matter as presented in resolution and preamble.
The resolution was signed by the farmers who were at the meeting. Here again the material is open to inspection by anybody, unless hon. members want me to take forty minutes to read it into the record. There are pages and pages of signatures of reeves, councillors, chairmen of school boards and so on from various municipalities.

No dead men?
Mr. BE'NTLEY: No dead men. I know them all personally and they are very much alive. I imagine that they were extremely alive at that meeting, because I know the temper of some of them.
No Liberals there?

Yes, there were Liberals there. The resolution was distributed throughout the country. I have received numerous letters from farmers in all parts of the constituency, and a lot of signed cards such as the one I have here. These were sent to me as a more simplified way of expressing their opinions.

Who
printed those cards?
They were done on typewriters by people who had to do it with one finger, the same as I have to when I have not a stenographer.
I was wondering whether it was something like the arms to China.

Not at all. These are honest farmers. They work hard to earn their living. They do not mind paying their way. The resolution on this card reads:
Whereas the prairie farmers' income tax forms are objectionable for the following reasons:
The form is impracticable, as it is impossible from the books kept by the majority of farmers for them to be completed with any degree of accuracy as the form contains too many details which are unknown by the taxpayer.
It is impossible for a farmer to give even a very rough estimate of feed fed io bvestock on the farm; therefore the inventory is impracticable.
Page five-net worth statement of the 1947 income tax form be deleted for the following reasons:
(1)	Too much of the farmers' personal business is involved which has no connection with income.
(2)	The prairie farmer is being singled out and obliged to answer personal questions not required from any other type of business.
Therefore be it resolved:
That the 1947 income tax form for prairie farmers be immediately recalled and that a more simplified form be submitted, and that the newr form shall not contain the net worth statement.
Some were inclined to be a little humorous when tackling this thing, and in a letter to one of the Saskatchewan papers one fellow suggested the following:
If Doctor McCann gets away with this form the next one may be worse, for instance the following may be added:
Beer used and consumed on farm during year	
Empty bottles returned (state value)	
Bottles picked up along the road (give separately)	
Empty bottles under the granary at end of year	
Where space insufficient add supplementary sheet.
Total	
These men are earnest about their dislike of this form and in this regard I should like to quote from a letter from one farmer who says:
Assets such as livestock can die at any time. Sometimes we hold grain for sale, but have to feed it if the weather goes against us or if we have other feeds spoil, etc. Cattle can drop in price so if we figure a steer at $100 now in our assets, he may only be worth $50 by the end of the year.
That is the sort of complaint I am receiving. I want to recommend to the government that, instead of sending out assessors, the government should recognize that there is a difficulty. People in Ottawa cannot make up a form for farmers to fill out when they know so little about the matter. If the government want to give the farmer an opportunity to be as honest as he wants to be they should set up some kind of continuing commission or body, call it a royal commission, an investigating body, a study body or whatever name you want to give it. This body could examine all phases of farm operations, all the things that take place on a farm to make income and all expenses of operation of a farm in all its infinite varieties across Canada. Then that body would be able to recommend the type of form
Farmers' Income Tax

which the farmer could fill in, with some feeling that he was doing justice to himself and paying his fair share.
I offer that suggestion in all earnestness and honesty to the government. I believe the government should accept that suggestion. There is no single member of the government, and I include the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) with his vast knowledge and tremendous ability, who is able at the present time to assess the difficulty of farmers in all parts of Canada in making up income tax forms.
I want to point out again that the people whom I have quoted, the people who attended this meeting, are responsible men. Many of them are reeves, councillors and members of public school boards and other local governing bodies. They are not dumbbells; they are able men. Many of them are entrusted with the expenditure of money raised in the form of local taxes. They know something about spending money for public needs. But they are not trained book-keepers or accountants and they cannot follow the various book-keeping intricacies required by some of these forms. But .give them an opportunity to do this in a simplified way and you will find that they are quite capable of accounting for their income and expenses and paying their honest share of the nation's revenue.

I am sure that visitors must have nothing but the greatest sympathy for members of parliament who have certainly earned their Easter recess after listening to the leader of the C.C.F. (Mr. Coldwell) tonight advocating that half-baked Hollywood mechanics should turn out crack pictures. In my opinion we should put the members of the film board to making a living where they might show some signs of doing something useful. Other speakers of the C.C.F. party have advocated lower taxation and tax exemption for the farmers.
That was never mentioned.

You have spoken for forty minutes and said less than I will say in five. I say, bring these men down from Saskatchewan who need a special book to make up their accounts and let them see what the government is spending on what the C.C.F. advocates, a glorified Hollywood here in Ottawa, and they will soon put a stop to spending this money on pictures and then will have less taxes to pay.

Before we proceed with the consideration of the supplementary estimates, would the minister take a moment to tell us the total amount of the main estimates voted last year, together with the total of the supplementaries now before us? If he will answer that, I want then to make two or three brief observations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The summary contained in the estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1949, which were tabled a week or two ago, shows that the total previously voted was $2,116,967,853.74, to which must be added the total of the further supplementaries now before the committee, which total $79,809,337.98, or a grand total of $2,196,777,191.72.

Mr. Chairman, about a week from today we shall come to the end of this fiscal year. As the minister has stated, the main estimates for this year amounted, in round figures, to $2,116,000,000, and the further supplementaries for the year amount to roughly $80,000,000, or a grand total of approximately $2,200,000,000. I am sure that every member wants the house to adjourn for Easter by tomorrow night if possible. But we have before us these supplementaries to pass. They include I do not know how many items. I can assure the minister that from this corner of the house there will be no unnecessary delay in considering these supplementaries. There are some very large items being put before us within a week of the end of the fiscal year. We shall want a simple statement explaining why at this stage of the fiscal year $80,000,000 more is required, and why in certain items there is a very large increase asked. I might mention some of them.
Item 564 shows $200,000 required for health of animals. I have no doubt there will be an easy' explanation of that item. Item 570 requires $250,000 for Prairie Farm Assistance Act administration. What we want to know in connection with these larger items is the total of the main estimate voted, and why this additional amount is necessary, just one week before the close of the fiscal year. Item 572 is for $6,500,000, "To authorize and provide for payment of subsidies on oats and1 barley used as feed for livestock-" listen to this-"under such regulations as may be approved by the governor in council". I suggest that that item ought not to be passed unless the government can tell us what regulations it is going to bring into effect with respect to that huge amount of money near the end of the fiscal year. I suggest, with all respect, that we should not be asked to pass

Supplementary Estimates
a lump sum like that without knowing what these regulations are which the government may bring into effect after we have gone home.
Let me mention two or three other items. Item 582, under the heading "special", is for $31,500,000 "To providle such amount as is necessary for payment to Canadian wheat board to reimburse that board1" for certain items. We shall want to be satisfied about the reason for these larger items.
Here is another one, item 588, $5,000,000 for "government's contribution to unemployment insurance fund". Why could a closer estimate not have been made of the requirements when the main estimates were brought down. How does it come about that within a week of the end of the fiscal year we are asked to provide these additional huge amounts?
One can pick out other items for $100,000, $198,000, $225,000, $250,000. I need not go over them all. Here are two others, items 638 and 639 under the heading "special", $548,000 for the Canadian Commercial Corporation and three-quarters of a million dollars for the Canadian wheat board, to reimburse the board for certain expenses incurred.
Item 649 under the heading "railway service" asks for $1,099,529.39, "additional amount in excess of the sum of $3,042,000 already appropriated, to authorize and provide for the payment from time to time during the fiscal year, 1947-48, to the Canadian National Railway Company", and so forth. I shall not go further on these points now.
I simply say to the minister that in the few hours remaining before we adjourn for Easter we want, the responsible ministers to give us a brief but clear explanation of these larger items and a justification for the additional amounts now being asked1 for. If a satisfactory explanation is given I think we shall all want to help the government get these supplementaries through as expeditiously as possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:

Director of Purchasing, Trade and Commerce
Compensation:
Annual: $10,000.

I do not remember, but it was substantial, perhaps seven or eight thousand a year. This was in 1939. During the war years he was one of the key men in the purchasing department of the Department of Munitions and Supply, in charge of the purchase of general supplies. I suppose in that capacity he purchased goods to a value of something over two billions of dollars on his own direct responsibility. When it was decided that the purchasing for the armed services would be transferred from the Department of Munitions and Supply-or the Department of Reconstruction and Supply, as it was then- to a continuing department, the functions were transferred to the Department of Trade and Commerce.
That department needed a man with experience and capacity to purchase on a scale required for the continuing services. Mr. Lowe seemed to be the obvious man. I might say that purchasing agents who are given the responsibility for purchasing on that scale are not to be picked off on street comers, and are not to be confused with those who ordinarilj7 buy a few hundred thousand dollars worth a year.
Purchasing for the armed services, even in peacetime, runs at a rate of a great many millions of dollars a year. It includes a variety of materials, the purchasing of which requires special knowledge. A purchasing agent must know sources of materials; he must know where they can be obtained. They are not obtained off the shelf; usually they must be manufactured to order. Mr. Lowe had that experience. He happened to be unique in that position. He was known as a man of great skill and much integrity, and he was appointed on the merit system because he was the best man available for the job, by any standards.
