Why would it not be possible to have all those figures in the column showing the total amount? We have just heard them read and they must have been ready.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The figures are only approximate. The figure which is being voted is just a round figure. I am informed that the statements have not yet been audited and there may be some slight variations when the auditors have completed their check.
Are the figures which the minister has just read virtually subsidies? They do not represent a deficit in trading account. How are they arrived at?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
These items are to reimburse the Canadian wheat board for losses suffered by the board during various crop years, where it can be shown either that the particular account has been closed out and the loss finally established, or that the eventual loss will be larger than the loss shown at the end of the crop year. Probably a good illustration is *the crown wheat account. This was the account established in September, 1943 when

Supply-Finance
the government closed the Winnipeg wheat market and took over, in the name of His Majesty, all the wheat then in commercial storage at a price of approximately $123 a bushel, basis No. 1 northern in store Fort William/Port Arthur. The account was replenished at a later date by purchases from the board's own wheat account. In general, the losses represent handling and storage charges.
That was a small one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was several million dollars. I am advised that that has been reimbursed to the extent of over $25,000,000, and this represents the balance.
The minister says that the amounts are mostly handling and storage charges, but I am not clear as to just how they came to be public charges.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am informed that this wheat was sold virtually at cost and, as I said, this represents handling and storage charges. In a sense, as my hon. friend says, it may be a subsidy to someone. It represents a loss which the Canadian wheat board took in handling this wheat.
I would point out to the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario that it was a subsidy to the people who bought the grain, not to the producers of the grain.
I am just anxious to find out what it is.

I should like to make an observation in two or three sentences. In my opinion it is confusing to mix up in this special item or in any estimate two distinct lines of activity in Canada's economic production. Here we have wheat, barley, oats, and then you switch into another line of activity altogether, namely, flax, which is a product that produces oil. The production of oil from sunflower seed and rapeseed, and even from flax seed will be of some magnitude. It will be something that will engage the attention of this house in the future. As oil production from the Pacific islands and Africa increases by leaps and bounds, it will come into direct competition with oil from sunflower seed and rapeseed and flax. I would suggest that in presenting these estimates in the days to come the wheat board be asked to separate these two lines of activity. There is a tremendous industry that is almost being subsidized in Canada, which at least gets a heavy depreciation allowance. I refer to the pressing out of oils. In the days to come, let us have those two items separate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I doubt if there will be items of this kind recurring. They all arise out of wartime activities authorized by order in council. They do not cover the ordinary operations of the wheat board. In this case the board is acting as the agent of the government in implementing various phases of government policy; but the main function of the wheat board, as the committee knows, is to act as marketing agent for the producers of wheat. Here they acted in a special capacity as agents for the government of Canada in carrying out special policies relating to the crown wheat account, the oats and barley equalization funds and other items. But the losses, if any, or the moneys which have been expended had to be taken care of out of public moneys, and not out of the proceeds of the sale of current crops of wheat.
These items go back to 1943. Why have deficits been allowed to accumulate so long? You are paying four per cent interest, which is more than was paid on victory bonds and many other government loans.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The interest rate is three per cent.

What is the need for so much haste in paying these accounts now? Why were they not paid previously? There is a $5,000,000 item at three per cent for 1943, crown wheat account. The oats equalization fund goes back to 1944. Why have these accounts been allowed to run on?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have paid something each year; and this is a final clean up, a series of adjusting items in these various accounts. Take, for instance, the crown wheat account. The deficit on the operations as of July 31, 1947, was over $31,000,000, on account of which there had been paid through different years, $25,861,000. There have been adjustments over the years, and this is a clean-up item. These were very large operations.
All the more reason why we should not be asked to pass them in a very few minutes when they have been allowed to run on now for five years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have been making payments on these accounts each year, and I am now trying to have them cleaned up.
Is the treasury board quite satisfied?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, and the final payment is subject to audit. That is why we are putting in a round figure slightly in excess of the statements furnished to us by the board.
Supply-Finance

As the minister has stated, this represents a clean-up. We cannot deal with these items intelligently in ten minutes. If we have any duty at all it is a far greater duty than just to pass these accounts sight unseen. They are in a very different category from many of these other items.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have a great deal of information I am quite ready to give and to answer any questions hon. members may ask. Let us spend the next fifteen minutes in discussing this item.
In my ignorance I must ask this question. To whom is the money owed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is owed to the Canadian wheat board, which has been acting in this case as agent for the government of Canada.
To whom in turn does the Canadian wheat board owe the money, and how did the Canadian wheat board come to have $31,000,000 on hand?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Either out of surplus moneys which the board had on hand or from bank loans which it made.
They must be bank loans if you are paying interest on them. To whom are you paying interest?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are paying interest to the farmer on the money which he has outstanding.

The farmer has not been getting any interest on the money owed to him. What is the amount which the wheat board owes to the farmers of this country? The government is paying this money to the wheat board at three per cent, which is more than the farmers have got on their money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am informed that this money benefits the farmer because it goes into the general fund of the wheat board. The amounts which are paid in cover the amounts which the board has disbursed, plus interest at three per cent from the time of disbursement. If this money is not paid the farmer could not get it.
If on the same type of transaction the wheat board had made a profit of several million dollars, would it come back to the government or go into the wheat board fund?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It would depend. In the oats and barley equalization fund it would have gone to the benefit of the farmer. But in this case the payments which were made

to the farmers at the time of delivery exceeded the amounts which were collected out of the export permits, and the government or the taxpayers made up the difference. If the transaction had resulted in a profit there would have been a distribution to the farmers. It was a case of "heads I win, tails you lose", so far as the farmer is concerned.
Is this why the farmers were not paid a more substantial initial pav-ment? Was it because the government wanted to use the farmers' money for something else?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This has no relation to the initial payment. The farmer gets everything coming to him, plus three per cent. His only quarrel could be whether the three per cent was high enough, and I would think it was.
Why do these items come in the supplementaries? Why were they not dealt with in the main estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The reason was to get as close as possible to the year to which it relates.
What are the main details of these items, so that we may get the over-all picture?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I gave the details a few moments ago.
The minister referred to the oats and barley equalization figures.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have already dealt with the crown wheat account. So far as the oats and barley equalization funds are concerned, there are four accounts here: barley for 1943; oats for 1944; oats and barley for 1945, and barley for 1946. All these losses arose because the advance equalization payments made to farmers at time of delivery in those years exceeded the amounts collected by the board out of equalization fees on exports. Equalization fees represented the difference between domestic ceiling prices and prices prevailing in export markets. In some years, of course, the funds showed a surplus which was or will be distributed to growers.
That means that we sold the oats and barley for less than we paid the farmers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. The farmer sold at the price ceiling, and received an advance equalization fee. That equalization fee was an estimate of what would be realized out of the oats and barley exported to the United States or elsewhere. When the oats and barley were exported the wheat board or the government made a charge for the export permit represent-

Supply-Justice
ing, broadly speaking, the difference between the domestic ceiling and the price received in the export market. The proceeds of these export permits were put into this equalization fund, and if the total exceeded the advance equalization fees paid to the farmers, there was a distribution made. It it was less, the farmer got his advance payment anyway, and we did not try to recover from him.

Had the wheat board, acting as agent for the government, sold more of the grain on the export market or charged the domestic consumers accordingly, you would not have had that loss. Because of these actions, the people who bought from the wheat board got the grain at that much lower price.
The minister is to give us some information on the flax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, 1944-45; the price realized by the board from the sales of flaxseed fell short of the price paid to the farmers at the time of delivery.
By how much?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: By the figure I gave; it is in Hansard.
That is for the two periods, 1944 and 1945?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a clean-up item, but I shall give the breakdown of it. The deficit on operations-this is the 1944 crop and the flax division-as at the 31st July, 1947, was 84.197.805.44. The amount which had already been paid to the board by the dominion and voted was 83.169,616.91. leaving a balance of $1,028,188.53, the vote that we are asking for in this supplementary vote.

Will the minister inform
some of the hon. members who seem to be concerned that it was the policy of the government to sell flaxseed at this price?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should be glad to do that. It is not my department. Perhaps that question might be addressed to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I have to find the money for it.
Inform the hon. members that it was the policy of the government to provide linseed oil and so forth from the flax to the consumers of Canada at prices below what it could have commanded elsewhere.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is perfectly right. The same principles applied to rapeseed and sunflower seed. The prices realized by the board on the sales of these seeds fell short of the 5849-163J
price paid to the farmers at the time of delivery. As the hon. member for Humboldt has pointed out, it was all pursuant to the maintenance of ceiling prices in Canada.
Will the minister give me the 1945 flaxseed figures?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. Deficit on operations to the 31st July, 1947, $2,537,433.04; due to the Canadian wheat board that amount, plus the interest.
In view of the fact that there was a loss of $6,500,000 on barley, was the fullest advantage taken that could be taken of the prices of malting barley in the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
What price?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not that information here; the going price, at the time the malting barley was sent down there.

58b To provide for a compassionate allowance to Mrs. Olevia Sullivan, widow of George Sullivan, deputy warden, Kingston penitentiary, equal to one-half of the gratuity to which deputy warden Sullivan would have been entitled had he chosen to resign, $6,234.38.

Will the minister
explain this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is an item of the Minister of Justice. He is not here. Perhaps I can get the information. The language of the item is fairly self-explanatory. I have some data on it here. This is an item which was approved in November, 1947, by the treasury board for inclusion in the 1947-1948 supplementary estimates. The circumstances are these. Deputy Warden Sullivan died suddenly on the 9th of March, 1941. He had reached the age of sixty-five on April 23, 1910. He was exempted from the provisions of P.C. 1/1561 for a period of one year. The reason for extension was the acute shortage of experienced officers at Kingston. He had completed over forty-six years service. Had he retired at age sixty-five, he would have received a gratuity of $12,112.50 and had he retired immediately prior to his death, the amount would have been 812,568.75. There are similar previous cases of officers who died in service and in which cases one-half of the allowable gratuity was paid. I do not know whether my
Supply-Labour

hon. friend wants the precedents; but there are a number of them.
Those people are not on the pension fund.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; this is a case where there was a gratuity available. It was one of those unfortunate cases where, by reason of the shortage which existed at the time, and he having continued in service, he got less than he would have received had he left the service and taken his cash gratuity.
Is it a lump sum or an annual payment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A lump sum.
